q: On a managed cluster such as EKS, which of these are still **your** responsibility? (select all)
options: Triggering control plane version upgrades
Keeping add-ons (CNI, CoreDNS, CSI drivers, controllers) compatible and updated
Running the API server across multiple AZs
etcd backups and quorum
RBAC and IAM access design
explain: The provider runs etcd and a highly available control plane. You decide when to upgrade, keep add-ons and nodes current, and design access, networking, workloads, backups and cost.

q: Your EKS cluster's pods suddenly fail to start with `failed to assign an IP address to container`. What is the most likely cause?
options: CoreDNS is overloaded
The AWS Load Balancer Controller is missing
The VPC CNI has run out of IP addresses in the subnets (or the instance's ENI/IP limit is reached)
Pod Security Admission blocks the pods
explain: With the VPC CNI, every pod consumes a VPC IP. Small subnets or per-instance ENI limits exhaust them. Fixes include larger or secondary CIDRs, prefix delegation and IPv6.

q: Which statement about Karpenter is correct?
options: It scales pods based on CPU like the HPA
It launches right-sized nodes directly for pending pods and consolidates underused nodes
It replaces the scheduler
It only works with Fargate
explain: Karpenter is a node autoscaler: it watches unschedulable pods, picks suitable instance types (including Spot) and launches them, and removes or replaces nodes when capacity can be packed more cheaply. The kube-scheduler still places pods.

q: Your control plane is on 1.31 and you must reach 1.34. What is the correct approach?
options: Upgrade the control plane directly to 1.34, then the nodes
Upgrade nodes to 1.34 first, then the control plane
Upgrade kubectl first; the cluster follows automatically
Upgrade the control plane one minor at a time (1.32, 1.33, 1.34), with nodes following within the allowed skew
explain: The control plane can only move one minor version per upgrade. Kubelets must never be newer than the API server and may lag by up to three minors, so nodes are upgraded after the control plane.

q: During a node group upgrade, draining one node hangs with `Cannot evict pod as it would violate the pod's disruption budget`. The Deployment has 1 replica and a PDB with `minAvailable: 1`. What is the proper fix?
options: Run at least two replicas spread across nodes and use `maxUnavailable: 1`
Drain with `--disable-eviction`
Delete the PDB permanently
Set `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 0`
explain: A PDB that allows zero disruptions can never be satisfied by evictions. Multiple replicas on different nodes plus a PDB allowing one disruption keep the service available while nodes are replaced. Deleting the PDB or bypassing eviction removes the protection.

q: How can you detect clients still using deprecated APIs before an upgrade removes them?
options: Run `kubectl get all`
Look at `kubectl version`
Check the `apiserver_requested_deprecated_apis` metric and scan manifests/Helm releases with tools like pluto or kubent
Wait for the upgrade and read the errors
explain: The API server records requests to deprecated APIs in a metric (and warns clients). Static scanners find deprecated apiVersions in Git and Helm release manifests. Fix them in source control before upgrading.

q: Which belong in a standard tenant namespace kit on a shared cluster? (select all)
options: LimitRange with default requests/limits
Pod Security Admission labels
Default-deny NetworkPolicy plus explicit allows
A ClusterRoleBinding granting the team `edit` everywhere
ResourceQuota
explain: Quotas, defaults, network isolation and pod security are per-namespace guardrails. Team access should be a RoleBinding in the team's namespace; a ClusterRoleBinding would grant it in every namespace.

q: A team's pods request 2 CPU each but use about 0.1 CPU. Why does this matter for cost?
options: High requests make pods slower
It does not: you pay for actual usage
Kubernetes charges per request
Nodes are packed by requests, so over-requesting forces more nodes than needed
explain: The scheduler reserves the requested CPU on a node regardless of use, and node autoscalers add nodes for pending pods based on requests. Right-sizing requests from real usage is the biggest cost lever.

q: You run Postgres in a StatefulSet. Which backup strategy is most appropriate?
options: Only Git, because GitOps can recreate everything
Database-native backups (e.g. WAL archiving/base backups via an operator, or a managed service's snapshots), with Velero or Git for the Kubernetes objects
Copying the PVC directory with kubectl cp nightly
Only Velero backups of the Kubernetes objects
explain: Git recreates configuration, not data. Volume snapshots of a running database are at best crash-consistent. Database-native backups give consistent, point-in-time recoverable data, and restores should be tested regularly.

q: What does a CustomResourceDefinition give you **without** any controller running?
options: A new API type with storage, schema validation, defaulting, RBAC, watch and kubectl support, but no behaviour when objects are created
A web UI for the resource
Automatic creation of Deployments for each custom resource
Nothing; the API rejects custom resources until a controller registers
explain: The API server fully serves the new type. Behaviour (creating Deployments, calling cloud APIs) comes from a controller that watches the resource and reconciles.

q: Which are properties of a well-written controller reconcile loop? (select all)
options: It reports observed state in the status subresource
Level-triggered: it computes actions from current desired and actual state, not from the event type
Idempotent: running it repeatedly has the same effect as running it once
It deletes and recreates all owned objects on every reconcile
It sets ownerReferences on objects it creates so garbage collection works
explain: Reconcilers converge state, tolerate missed events, set owners and report status. Recreating everything each time would cause needless restarts and downtime.

q: When is writing your own operator a good idea?
options: To avoid learning Helm
When you have operational logic (failover, backups, multi-step upgrades) to automate across many instances and no existing operator fits
For every microservice your team owns
Whenever you need to template a few YAML files per environment
explain: Operators are software to maintain, secure and upgrade. Templating is better handled by Helm or Kustomize; operators earn their keep by encoding repeated operational knowledge.

q: You are a backend engineer who deploys services to Kubernetes but does not run clusters. Which certification is the most natural first step?
options: CKAD
KCSA
CKA
CKS
explain: CKAD focuses on designing, deploying, configuring and troubleshooting applications. CKA adds cluster administration (kubeadm, etcd, node troubleshooting); CKS requires a passed CKA.
